title: Tracking states’ unprecedented redistricting efforts
body: Republicans have come out ahead in the national fight over congressional maps in what could be a major boon to their efforts to protect their narrow majority ahead of the midterm elections. Legal skirmishes over the maps continued up to the last minute. Democrats secured a late victory in Missouri after that state’s Supreme Court blocked a new Republican-drawn map , and the US Supreme Court refused to reinstate it . The result is that November’s elections in the state will be conducted under a map with at least two winnable seats for Democrats instead of just one. The court battles came against the backdrop of the Supreme Court’s blockbuster decision earlier this year to gut a significant part of the Voting Rights Act. The ruling led to new maps in several Republican states, boosting the number of new GOP-friendly districts created this year. Those developments marked a major shift in Republicans’ favor in the battle that President Donald Trump and his party launched last year. It had previously appeared headed towards a virtual draw, with Democratic states all but canceling out Republican redraws. While Republicans might not win every district they’ve targeted on their new maps, the shifts will give them a boost as they try to hold the House in a challenging political environment. With a historically tight House of Representatives , redistricting has become a critical tactic to shaping the midterm races. Redistricting, or the process of redrawing congressional district boundaries, typically takes place just once a decade , as states respond to updated population counts after the decennial census . The redistricting process is different in every state. In some places, state legislators can redraw the map on their own, and all that’s needed is the political will. In other states, the redraw might require changing the constitution, a lengthier process which often involves a direct vote of the people. Overall, Republicans began the cycle with more opportunities to gain seats through new maps than Democrats did. Republicans have full control of government in more states and many Democratic states have ceded the map-drawing power to independent commissions, moves some of them have now reversed. And now that mid-decade redistricting has become another political tool, it shows no signs of slowing down. Maryland voters will consider a measure this November that would give Democrats more freedom to draw a new map and several other states could have new maps before 2028. EDITOR’S NOTE: This story has been updated with additional information. —CNN’s Molly English, Arit John and Dianne Gallagher contributed to this report. title: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape
body: Exit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing Full report: Coalition talks loom as Israel exit polls suggest Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs tied The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival. In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls , the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that. The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, which are projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored. The exit polls placed Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s governing coalition tied. Though the prime minister’s Likud party could still be the strongest single party, neither side has enough to get 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament for a majority. If confirmed by actual results, that would give Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, discretion over who he asks first to try to form a government. If one candidate cannot succeed in six weeks, the challenge is passed on to the next option. It could be an extremely long process, and all this time Netanyahu’s coalition would stay on in a caretaker role. Eisenkot could argue he has a chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List). They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has a Jewish Zionist deputy, he has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, and [Itamar] Ben-Gvir in this election”. However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government. Negotiations with the Joint List, with 11 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinian Israeli citizens, who are exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation. Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks. “Laying down conditions won’t work with the Joint List,” Shbita said. “We will negotiate as equals because we need each other.” In the absence of an agreement with one or both of the Palestinian groupings, it is possible that Eisenkot could try to govern as a minority government, with informal vote-by-vote agreements that would keep the new coalition afloat. It would be an unstable solution, making another election more than likely. That would provide Netanyahu the opportunity to rally support among conservative Israeli Jews and claim to have been vindicated in his campaign slogan, “the Right or Palestine”, which rhymes in Hebrew. Netanyahu has looked beaten before over his three decades at or near the top, and staged a comeback each time with the aid of his unparalleled tactical skills as a dealmaker. No one is yet ruling out another breathtaking political escape. But this time, if he does bounce back, he would owe his resurrection to his avowed political enemies for dropping him a lifeline rather than make historic compromises across Israel’s deep racial divide. Speaking from the Joint List victory party in Nazareth in the early hours of Wednesday, one party official said: “The Zionist opposition will have to choose between supremacy and building democracy.”

title: The shocking rise of rib remodelling: ‘I wanted that hourglass shape’
body: It involves the fracturing of a patient’s ribs, before they spend three months laced into a corset. Some of those who have had this cosmetic procedure say it is like being ‘hit by a bus’. Why is it becoming more popular? D aniela Cesin was 14 when she began thinking about her looks. “I was a little bit chubby and I started to work out at home and lose weight. I saw the difference in my body: my abs, the muscles in my arms, and I started liking it,” she says. By 31, she had the slim, toned body she had hoped for, but something was still missing. “I wanted to have that guitar hourglass shape.” In August, Cesin travelled from Miami, where she has lived for the past 15 years, to her native Venezuela for liposuction and a fat transfer to her hips. She met her cosmetic surgeon for the first time the day before the procedure, and he realised she didn’t have enough fat to go ahead with it. Instead, he offered to perform RibXcar: a rib remodelling surgery that would involve fracturing three of her lower ribs on each side and binding them in a corset for three months, to set the ribs in a new position and give her a wasplike waist. “I was like: ‘No, no, no, I don’t want to do anything with the ribs,’” she says. The idea of breaking the bones around her vital organs sounded a lot more invasive than a breast augmentation, which she had 10 years ago, or a rhinoplasty (nose surgery) and blepharoplasty (eyelid surgery), which she had two years ago. Also, she had never heard of the procedure. But after the consultation, she decided to trust her surgeon. Cesin had already paid for flights and taken three weeks off from her job as a sales director. The next day she was anaesthetised, and her surgeon used an ultrasound to locate the ribs, made six small incisions in her back, and inserted a vibrating tool to create greenstick fractures – an incomplete bone break – on each rib. When she came to she was wearing a black corset with small knobs on each side that she could tighten to her preferred measurements. The recovery has been uncomfortable. It was initially hard to stand or lie down without help, and there was soreness from the incisions. The first week, Cesin barely slept. “Your body doesn’t get used to any position, so every hour I would wake up.” But the worst part has been eating while wearing her corset, which must remain on for 23 hours a day; this causes acid reflux. Despite her discomfort, when we speak six weeks after her surgery, she is pleased with the eight centimetres she has shaved off her waist. Cesin is one of a small but growing number of women choosing to fracture their ribs for an hourglass shape. To achieve this look, women previously underwent riskier rib removal techniques, which reduce the protective bone barrier for the liver and spleen. Kazbek Kudzaev, a plastic surgeon in Russia, realised in 2017 that he could achieve similar aesthetic results when he moved the ribs with a drill until one side fractured, then bound the body in a corset while they healed. Since his discovery, surgeons in countries including Colombia, Korea and France have refined the technique. Today, it takes about an hour and is performed under general anaesthesia as a day-surgery treatment. It is touted as a noninvasive procedure, but many of the women I interviewed described feeling as if they had been “hit by a bus” after surgery. And there are serious risks. These include standard surgical complications, such as allergic reactions to the anaesthesia, blood clots, wound infections and seromas (pockets of fluid that build up under the skin). But also more specific dangers, including a collapsed lung, known as a pneumothorax; and a haemothorax, where blood collects in the space between the chest wall and the lungs. Both of these are potentially fatal. Sandip Hindocha, a consultant plastic surgeon at the Private Clinic on Harley Street in London, is sceptical about the procedure. “If a patient came to my clinic and said this is what I want to do, I’d be asking the question: ‘Why do you want to do that? And why do you want to make such a permanent change to your body?’” He references a paper published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, which states that between 2018 and 2024, out of 2,351 patients who had rib remodelling, there was an overall complication rate of 3.7%. “That’s not a small number,” he says. “If we did a breast augmentation, you wouldn’t expect a complication rate like that.” The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), doesn’t endorse the procedure. Former president Nora Nugent points out that it is relatively new, “with limited data available on long-term results and it requires advanced body contouring skills as well as the ability to treat any potential complications. It may be something that UK/BAAPS plastic surgeons bring into their practices in due course but it is not available at the moment.” The procedure isn’t typically offered to cisgender women over the age of 40, because of the increased chance of them having osteoporosis, which can cause the bones to fully break rather than fracture. Another complication for patients is that gaining weight can cause your body to change shape again, so pregnancy can affect the results. The procedure “needs to be done with a surgeon who has a lot of experience in it,” says Hindocha. “Maybe a surgeon that also does chest wall reconstruction.” In the UK, plastic surgeons are advised to give patients a cooling-off period of at least two weeks to weigh up the risks and potential consequences of having any procedure. But Hindocha worries that patients are sometimes opting for rib remodelling with less time for reflection, despite the permanence of the change. “If you put an implant in and later you don’t want it, you can, worst case scenario, remove it,” Hindocha says. Whereas the ribs are “a structural, rigid part of you that you cannot reverse.” T hroughout history, waistlines have expanded and shrunk. Between the 16th and 19th centuries, corset wearing and tight-lacing became a symbol of beauty for the “leisure class” (the restrictive garments made physical labour impossible). The engineered hourglass shape fell out of fashion in the 1920s, but made a comeback with Marilyn Monroe, before slender, androgynous frames gained popularity from the 60s to the 90s. In the 2010s, the extreme curves of the Kardashians became the defining silhouette. In recent years, tinier, waif-like frames have become popular on TikTok and Instagram, but a highly defined waist is also considered desirable. This is thanks, among other things, to the multibillion-dollar shapewear industry ; global access to Instagram and filters; and easily streamed online workout videos that focus on creating a slim, hourglass silhouette through targeted training. But now there are adverts on social media for permanent surgical options too. In July, 10 Australian influencers, who have made names for themselves globally on shows including Married at First Sight and Below Deck, prompted headlines with a trip to Bali. They were there for a brand collaboration with a rib recontouring practice called Snatched Waist. The clinic they visited looked more like a spa than a surgeon’s office and, post-surgery, the influencers were soon lounging by the pool, showing off their narrow waists on Instagram. Not everyone is sunbathing in a bikini after the procedure. When Sophia woke up from her rib remodelling procedure in November 2025, she expected to be transferred to her Beverly Hills hotel room, a little sore but ready for recovery. Instead, she was surrounded by emergency medical technicians, who were putting her on to a stretcher to take her to hospital by ambulance. The next thing she remembers is lying in a hospital bed, hooked up to an electrocardiogram and an intravenous drip. A CT scan showed Sophia had suffered a pneumothorax: 25% of one of her lungs had collapsed. She was put on oxygen and monitored for six hours before being released. Although she had signed all the consent forms for the procedure, “it was completely shocking to me,” she says. For at least a month, Sophia had a deep pain in her lung and some shortness of breath. She had to return to the hospital after some fluid build up, but eventually started feeling better. The pain from the surgery itself subsided after about three weeks: coughing and sneezing was no longer agonising. And she was able to return to her office job and hike in her corset at the weekends. Sophia is transgender and chose the procedure to feminise her body, by narrowing her torso, which she felt was too wide. She began consultations for the procedure in August last year, with the surgeon planning to fracture ribs 10, 11 and 12. But by the time of her surgery in November, the surgeon felt confident he could achieve better results by going even further up the ribcage, ultimately operating on five ribs on each side. Sophia knew this would increase her risk of a pneumothorax, but was willing to take the chance. “I didn’t start transitioning until I was 47 and I feel as if I’m playing catch up, because I’m so old, and testosterone was running rampant all those decades,” she says. “That’s why gender-affirming procedures are really important to me.” The final results weren’t what she had hoped for though. “It was a bit underwhelming.” In September this year, she went for a second round of rib remodelling with Leif Rogers, a different surgeon in Pasadena and Beverly Hills, California. Rogers removed cartilage from the anterior side of her ribcage on ribs three to 10. On rib four, he cut sections out and secured them with titanium plates and screws. Sophia had a breast augmentation at the same time, as the inframammary incisions were already open. When she emails to update me a week and a half after her second surgery, although there has been no collapsed lung this time, she says: “Recovery has been significantly more painful, and I am experiencing more shortness of breath.” Despite the risks, Rogers expects skeletal remodelling to take off : that includes rib remodelling, clavicle shortening and pelvic widening. “Versions of it have existed for quite some time,” he says. “Limb lengthening and shortening has been around for a long time. Of course, we change the bony skeleton of the face all the time, but other than that we haven’t changed the torso very much. The changing of the skeleton of the body is a little bit newer, as for a long time people used to just put their hands up and say: ‘Too bad, this is the way you’re built.’” So why now? “The techniques have got way better. And there’s marketing for it out there.” In the US, he says, medical insurance often covers the procedure for transgender patients, “because they consider it a medical condition to have gender dysphoria. And I think on top of that, it’s just social media. Social media makes everything explode.” Rogers says the Kardashians have been highly influential. “I think Kim was part of why we wanted a big butt, and then she lost a lot of weight, so everyone wants to be like Kim, right?” In 2022, Kim Kardashian attended the Met Gala after losing a considerable amount of weight, in a sparkling dress once worn by Monroe. Her slender figure coincided with a growing movement towards thinness, a rejection of the body positivity movement of the 2010s, and the advent of the Ozempic era, when the diabetes drug became popular as a weight-loss treatment. A controversial 2022 New York Post article was headlined: “ Bye-bye booty: Heroin chic is back ”. On TikTok, people had begun measuring their waists using A4 sheets of paper, phones and Apple headphone wires, showing off their Barbie-like proportions. “We have always done very demanding things for beauty,” says Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and author of the 2018 book Perfect Me, who mentions foot binding and extreme corsetry. “But they were always about adornment. I think what’s different with the global ideal now is that increasingly things are becoming normalised and naturalised. We’re seeing things that are purely about adornment being recategorised as health and hygiene, and then they become invisible, and if you don’t do them you start to look abnormal,” she says. “It becomes about standard presentation.” As we move from a text-based culture to a visual culture, increasingly, “who we are is how we look,” she says, “and that is a form of identity that is a massive and dramatic change, but one that’s snuck up on us, that we don’t talk about enough. So the visual is becoming the dominant way of presenting ourselves, being ourselves and thinking about ourselves.” Elizabeth Rivera trained in high level gyms alongside American football players, baseball players and Ms Bikini Olympia, to try to reach her beauty ideal. This was the X-frame specific to bodybuilders: broad shoulders, prominent glutes and a small waist. For her, she says: “That looks like health. That’s a visible indication of discipline.” Rivera was “busting ass”, trying to reach this aesthetic ideal, but “it was not working for me. And I was making myself very sick from overtraining.” Rivera is a 35-year-old licensed masseuse and she has lipedema, a chronic condition that causes abnormal fat deposits, which can be painful and are resistant to diet or exercise. “Once I accepted that my inability to lose fat wasn’t my fault, I said: ‘OK, I can accept that.’ But I still would like to have a smaller abdomen. I still would like to have more of an hourglass. So surgery was the next option.” A friend had recently had her ribs remodelled, and Rivera was impressed with the results. She stands up halfway through our Zoom call to show off her waist. It’s objectively tiny, and the effect is exaggerated by her breast implants and petite Brazilian butt lift (BBL). “I can go most places in Chicago [where she lives], and there’s no one shaped like me. And I’m not saying that in a bad way. I’m saying that because it looks more extreme with the ribs, it’s noticeable.” In Miami where Cesin lives, she says she doesn’t feel her shape puts her in the minority. There, cosmetic surgery is widely accepted and expected. “The girls in Miami, all of them look the same, because it’s a lot of fillers, a lot of buttocks, a lot of surgery and BBLs,” she says, adding that it’s easy, as a result, to get carried away. But she doesn’t want to end up like that. “People say rib remodelling was a little bit extra, that I didn’t need to do anything, but it makes me happy, so that’s why I did it. But I’m done. No more surgeries.” Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘It’s the gay Titanic!’ Inside La Bola Negra, the maximalist queer spectacular bound for Oscars glory
body: Oozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it up W hen Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo – the directing duo known in their native Spain as “Los Javis” – began writing their queer epic La Bola Negra, they weren’t thinking about whether it would be stylish (which it is) or win numerous awards (which it has) or capture what they refer to as “the anti-fascist zeitgeist” (which it does). Instead, they thought only of scale. “I’m done with LGBTQ+ movies being niche,” says Ambrossi. “I was like, ‘Let’s make the biggest, gayest war movie ever .’” Job done. At Cannes this year, the best director prize was awarded jointly to them and to Paweł Pawlikowski, who made the Thomas Mann road trip film Fatherland . La Bola Negra is now an Oscars frontrunner, with best picture and best director nominations all but guaranteed. Brimming with panache, the movie darts back and forth between three stories set in Spain: in 1932, a young man applying for membership of an exclusive casino is rejected on the grounds of his suspected homosexuality; in 1937, a callow nationalist soldier develops tender feelings for the injured republican prisoner under his watch; and in 2017, a queer historian inherits an unfinished story by Federico García Lorca. That story lends the movie its title and provides the thread that sews its strands together. Throw in spectacular set pieces, Ken Russell-style visual flair, cameos from a blond-wigged Penélope Cruz and a Spanish-speaking Glenn Close, and the result is a maximalist collage where the Spanish civil war sits side-by-side with Grindr hook-ups. “We loved imagining scenes that you don’t usually have in queer movies,” says Ambrossi, citing the spectacular opening sequence in which a Spanish village is bombed by Italian fascists. “A lot of people have said they’ve been missing something like this. They want to buy popcorn and be given a big movie like Titanic.” His eyes widen. “This is the gay Titanic!” Relaxing at a corner table in the restaurant of a London hotel, Los Javis represent a study in contrasts. Ambrossi is 42, dinky and loquacious, his impish face crowned with a laurel of curls. He leans forward as he talks, arms folded on the white tablecloth. The taller, taciturn Calvo, 35, is gravely handsome. Battling jet lag, he repeatedly stretches his limbs like a cat, sneaking a glance at himself in the mirror next to the table as he does so. Both men have black caterpillar eyebrows, as well as cheekbones that could double as clothing rails. On this chilly autumn morning, Los Javis could do with some extra layers. They rub their bare arms furiously until an assistant arrives bearing hoodies. Then again, maybe the three of us have goosebumps not from the cold but from discussing their film. Ambrossi approves of this theory: “There’s a trend on TikTok where people video themselves – ‘This is us before watching La Bola Negra’ – and then it cuts to afterwards when they’re crying and hugging. All this togetherness from the cinematic experience is beautiful.” No wonder Los Javis insisted on an extended theatrical window for their film before selling the US rights to Netflix. La Bola Negra will remain in US cinemas for 47 days, a record for the streaming platform. Even Scorsese didn’t get that. The movie also marks a personal breakthrough for the pair, who first met when they were actors. “Friends who read the script said to us, ‘Oh, you’re going there? ’” recalls Ambrossi. “We’ve been writing together for 13 years about LGBTQ+ characters but it has always been, like, lesbians, trans women …” Previous collaborations include their 2017 debut film, Holy Camp!, which they adapted from La Llamada, their stage musical about a summer camp staffed by nuns. In one scene, God materialises to sing I Will Always Love You. Their 2023 series La Mesías (now streaming on Mubi ) is a hypnotically bizarre tale of Christian pop stars, extraterrestrials and bad parenting. But no gay men. What took them so long? “Sometimes you don’t want to talk about yourself,” offers Calvo, speaking up at last. “Many queer creators have projected themselves into other characters. Pedro Almodóvar, Lorca with The House of Bernarda Alba, Michael Patrick King with Sex and the City.” He flashes a rare smile. “Good show.” Ambrossi identifies a psychological dimension to the delay: “It’s true you don’t want to be too on-the-nose. But you start wondering if there is also another reason.” In the 1932 strand of the film, the elite casino members use a system of black and white balls to vote on admitting newcomers. The black ball for no– la bola negra – becomes a symbol of queer generational shame and rejection that must be wrestled with. Is it shame, then, that kept Ambrossi from addressing his own sexuality in his work? “In my case, yes. I wasn’t ready to talk about desire or sex because I felt ashamed in some way.” He and Calvo were already friends with their compatriot and hero Almodóvar, whose company El Deseo, meaning Desire, co-produced La Bola Negra. “I told Pedro, ‘I don’t deal well with desire.’ He looked at me and said, ‘You need to start.’ That’s when it clicked: if you don’t deal explicitly with desire, you are missing life.” Perhaps that is why the word “explicit” crops up several times in Ambrossi’s conversation today: having been out as a gay man but under the radar in his work, he is eager now to emphasise the ways in which La Bola Negra is defiant or unequivocal. One aspect is the casting of gay actors in gay roles, most notably the Bambi-eyed singer Guitarricadelafuente, who makes his screen debut as the lovestruck soldier. “It’s not that straight actors can’t play gay,” says Calvo. “There are no rules in art. But …” Ambrossi jumps in: “We like to do it this way. When I was 10, I watched Rupert Everett in My Best Friend’s Wedding. I wasn’t sure I was gay, but I knew he was like me. There was a truth in his eyes that I want to get in my movies.” He sighs. “Rupert Everett was so brave. He should have been James Bond.” Calvo had an unhappy experience as a young gay actor. “I was a teenager playing a gay role on TV,” he says. “When it finished, I didn’t get many auditions. I was advised to cut my hair, not paint my nails.” A short back and sides didn’t help, though. “I guess people could still tell. So I decided to write roles for actors who don’t have space in the industry.” Once the pair began dating as well as working together, the two-headed queer celebrity phenomenon of Los Javis was born. They were playwrights, film-makers, actors and reality TV participants, including regular judges on the Spanish version of Ru Paul’s Drag Race. Being an indispensable part of Spanish cultural life came at a price. Calvo points to this now as one of the reasons he and Ambrossi separated during the making of La Bola Negra. “People would talk to me in the plural all the time, ‘It was nice to meet you guys.’ I’d be like, ‘Huh? I’m standing alone here.’ I felt I’d lost my individuality.” Spain didn’t cope well with the breakup. “It was a big deal,” Calvo admits. “There were cameras outside my door for a month.” Keen to move on, Ambrossi displays a flicker of irritation: “I think we’ve passed through this conversation. Imagine everyone talking about your ex forever! We love to write and direct together and we’re going to keep doing that.” The matter is closed. After all the diversifying and cross-platforming, Los Javis have reached their Pokémon-style final evolution. “From now on, we want to focus on movies,” says Calvo. No regrets, though. “The other things were important in making a statement,” Ambrossi points out. “I grew up thinking directors should be serious and monolithic. We represented a new way.” Calvo lifts a finger: “A non-binary way,” he says. “We don’t see life as stiff. We mix genres. A more flexible time is coming. Take the work seriously but not yourself.” Before they go, there is a line in La Bola Negra that I ask them to unpack. When the modern-day researcher Alberto asks the Lorca scholar played by Glenn Close for advice on what he should do with the pages of that incomplete story, she tells him: “You’ve inherited something and you don’t know what to do with it. You are truly a Spaniard.” Calvo is happy to help. “In Spain, we always have to be reminded by foreigners that we have a rich, interesting culture and history,” he says. Ambrossi elaborates: “It is as if pride is shameful. When someone is doing well and winning awards all over Spain, people are like, ‘Hmm. That’s not very Spanish.’ Unless it’s football.” Where does that attitude come from? “Maybe religion,” muses Calvo. “Maybe dictatorship.” Does it apply to them? Are they destined to underplay their triumphs for ever? They offer their best you’ve-got-to-be-kidding looks, then answer in unison: “Not us.” La Bola Negra is in UK cinemas from 6 November.

title: Jio shares surge 21% in market debut after blockbuster India IPO
body: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Jio Platforms, billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Indian telecom and digital services unit backed by Meta and Google, surged 21% in its stock market debut on Wednesday after raising $3.2 billion in India’s largest and most subscribed IPO, which attracted more than $77 billion in investor bids. The shares opened at ₹1,358 (about $14) apiece, up from their IPO price of ₹1,119 (around $12). That valued Jio at around ₹12.5 trillion (around $131.9 billion), making it India’s second-most valuable listed company after its parent, Reliance Industries, which is worth about ₹16 trillion (around $168.6 billion). In 2020, when Meta and Google invested, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion ( about $65 billion at the time). The offering, which ran from October 21 to 22, drew bids for 22.19 times the shares on sale, according to exchange data. More than 13.8 million people applied. That made it India’s most subscribed stock offering on record, reflecting strong investor demand for shares in the country’s largest telecom operator. In 2016, Jio entered what was then a crowded Indian telecom market, offering free data and low-cost services. That helped it quickly win customers from established operators including Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It has since become the country’s largest telecom operator. Akash Ambani (pictured above), Jio Platforms’ managing director, said at Wednesday’s listing ceremony that its platforms serve more than 540 million customers. Jio’s prices are now broadly in line with those of its rivals’, but its business has expanded into broadband , cloud services , and AI . Akash, Mukesh Ambani’s eldest son, has taken on a larger role in Jio as his father gradually hands more responsibility to the next generation of Reliance’s leadership. At the listing ceremony, he said he wants Jio to become a global technology company. “My dream is that one day, when the world counts its great technology companies, one of them will be from India, and that company will be called Jio Platforms Limited,” he said. Jio made ₹300.5 billion (about $3.2 billion) in profit on revenue of ₹1.47 trillion (around $15.5 billion) in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with both figures up about 15% from a year earlier. In the June quarter, Jio’s revenue grew nearly 12% and profit rose 9%. From the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion (about $2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remainder going toward general corporate purposes. Jio had total borrowings of ₹613.7 billion (around $6.5 billion) as of June 30. Jio drew billions of dollars from American investors during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion , while Google put in $4.5 billion . General Atlantic, Silver Lake, and Vista Equity Partners were among the other investors that backed the company. None sold shares in the IPO, which consisted entirely of newly issued shares. title: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
body: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions . Yet according to Anthropic’s S-1 , none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures. While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO. Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale. According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30. As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company. Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit. But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion. Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years. Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic. The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times , and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 5.6%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from the Anthropic through 2033. While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on. The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does. title: Who’s really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO?
body: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term. As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets. Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley. But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board. First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety. That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors. Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi. There is one vacancy on the board. Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity. The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors. The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs. There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now. The existing members will themselves choose who fills it. Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors. If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock. Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT. When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote. The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict. We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was not being candid with them. Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place. Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power. At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries. The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain. At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board. If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control. title: OpenAI reportedly plans to buy Google’s TPU chips alongside Nvidia
body: A purchase of Google’s tensor processing units would give one of Nvidia’s biggest customers a rival chip supplier. OpenAI plans to buy AI chips from Google, The Information reported on Tuesday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The financial terms and other details of the planned purchase were not disclosed. We have not independently verified the report, and OpenAI declined to comment to Reuters, which followed up on the story, while Google did not immediately respond to the news agency. The chips are Google’s tensor processing units (TPUs), processors built specifically for AI work. A purchase would mark a shift for OpenAI, which is among the largest buyers of Nvidia’s graphics processors. It would also give Google a major customer for chips it has only recently started selling. In April, Google said it would sell TPU hardware directly to a small group of customers, who can run the chips in their own data centres. Demand has grown on the back of deals with customers including Anthropic. In fact, Google has sold so much TPU capacity that its own researchers have had to wait for access. Alphabet’s finance chief, Anat Ashkenazi, has said the company expects to book a small share of TPU sales revenue by the end of this year. Most of it will come in 2027, she said. OpenAI and Google compete in AI products and search, but their business ties are growing. Last week, OpenAI said its frontier models would become available on Google Cloud , after a similar move with Amazon Web Services . The relationship has shifted before. In June 2025, Reuters reported that OpenAI had begun renting Google’s chips. Soon after, however, OpenAI said it had no active plans to use them in its products. At the same time, OpenAI is building its own hardware. In June, it unveiled its first custom AI chip, designed with Broadcom, and plans to put it into use by the end of this year. The report comes as tech groups spend heavily on AI computing. Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet plan to spend as much as $600bn combined on AI infrastructure this year, according to Reuters. Alphabet reports its quarterly results later today. title: Oracle will offer Cerebras AI computers in its cloud from 2027
body: The deal gives the Nvidia challenger another big cloud customer, after OpenAI and Amazon Web Services. Oracle will offer cloud services running on Cerebras’ AI computers in its data centres from 2027, the companies said. Cerebras, which went public in May, is expected to triple revenue next year to almost $3B, but investors worry about its place in a market Nvidia dominates. Oracle will offer cloud services built on Cerebras Systems’ AI computers in its data centres, Bloomberg reported . The deal gives the young Nvidia challenger another large customer. Cerebras builds each chip from a whole silicon wafer, the disk normally cut into many smaller processors. It says this lets its systems answer AI requests much faster than rivals. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure plans to offer the service in 2027, the companies said on Tuesday . Oracle did not say how much Cerebras hardware it will use. “ AI inference demands choice, ” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. Cerebras already counts OpenAI and Amazon Web Services as customers. Analysts expect it to triple its revenue next year to almost $3B, from less than $1B this year, according to Bloomberg. Investors still worry that Cerebras is chasing a small niche in a market where Nvidia’s products bring in close to $100B in sales each quarter. Shares in Cerebras, which listed in May , rose about 9.5% on Tuesday. Oracle made the announcement at its annual AI World conference, alongside deals with Nvidia and Intel. It also buys Arm’s own chips . Oracle plans to spend $70B on capital projects in the year to May 2027, after spending $55.7B the year before. Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. title: ‘I want them to get better’: Remote CEO Job van der Voort on AI
body: Job van der Voort told the TNW Podcast he made an AI course mandatory at Remote. The payroll company is profitable and has no plans to go public. TNW’s Cristian Dina (left) and Remote CEO Job van der Voort at HumanX in Amsterdam, 23 September 2026 Remote chief executive Job van der Voort wants his staff to be 10 times more effective a year from now, because their AI tools will be 10 times more effective too. The company runs payroll and hires staff in other countries for its customers. Rather than replace people with AI, he wants to train the ones it has, he told TNW. Van der Voort, who is Dutch, studied neuroscience and left his PhD to start a company with a friend. It ran out of money fast, he said. He then joined GitLab, where staff worked remotely all over the world, and hiring and paying them across countries proved a constant struggle. He left GitLab in January 2019 and started Remote a week later. He runs it with co-founder Marcelo Lebre . He spoke to Cristian Dina at HumanX in Amsterdam on 24 September. It is the latest episode of the TNW Podcast, after Boomi’s Steve Lucas , Daytona’s Ivan Burazin and Glean’s Arvind Jain . The full conversation is in the video below. Remote has about 2,000 employees and keeps growing. Van der Voort does not plan to grow the workforce much, or to shrink it, he said. When a team gets busier, the first thing people ask for is another hire. They make good arguments, which is what makes it tricky. Remote told staff to try solving the problem with AI first. “It works as a good forcing function to say, well, you cannot hire more people, right? Because then people have to look for solutions.” Job van der Voort, Remote chief executive Some people at Remote took to AI quickly. A large group did not, he said. So Remote built an AI course and made it compulsory. It has since made the course free for anyone as AI for Actual Work . Some payroll teams thought tools like these could not work for them, because they had done the job the same way for 20 years. Remote still fights that, he said. His answer is not to fire them and hire people who already use AI. “The people that I hire, I want to take care of them and I want them to get better.” Job van der Voort Most of Remote’s customers are startups that employ knowledge workers. Van der Voort said Remote has not seen them hire faster or slower. AI companies are the exception: they are growing “like crazy,” he said. The last big shift was the wave of layoffs in 2022, when venture funding started to fall. Since then the market has been stable. No customer has told Remote it is replacing an employee with an AI agent, he said, though Remote does not always know why someone leaves. Companies are trying to make their people more effective, and most are “not on the AI bandwagon yet,” he said. The change he does see is between employees and contractors. Demand for independent contractors has gone up “massively,” he said, because AI companies need people to label data and give feedback to their models. It began with simple labelling. Now many are PhDs who do the work alongside their research. He expects that market to keep growing for the next few years. “What’s going to happen beyond that I don’t know. I don’t think anybody knows.” Job van der Voort Remote is profitable and cash flow positive, he said. Its last funding round was a Series C in 2022, and it has raised no private capital since, because it has no need to. It has no plans to go public or to sell. Its customers run from Burger King to Anthropic, he said, and number in the tens of thousands. Its own staff are in 90 countries, with the largest group, about 20%, in the US. Remote can be accessed through an MCP server, so authorised agents like Claude or ChatGPT can work with it within the user’s permissions. Remote is building agents that automate payroll tasks across countries, such as chasing staff to submit expenses on time. Remote does come up against Deel, Oyster and Rippling in some deals, he said. But its main rivals are local payroll firms that have done the same work for two decades, and sometimes an office of accountants. Labour law differs in every European country, and the challenge grows as Remote gets bigger, he said. He is not optimistic. “I think it’s bad for Europe that we have so much complicated rules around hiring and employing people and setting up businesses.” Job van der Voort His next company could be in robotics, because he thinks software is “sort of getting solved,” he said. He thinks about it every day. For now, he plans to keep growing Remote. His advice to graduates is to join a startup, fail a lot and keep going, because “the way to win is basically to just stick around.” Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. title: Join the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Ghost in the Machine! $2,850 in Prizes Across 21 Winners.
body: Week 4 of our Hacktoberfest DEV Challenges starts today, and it's our final challenge of the series ! Running through October 31 , the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4 gives you the week to build, wrapping up on Halloween night just as Día de los Muertos begins. 🎃🌼 This year's Hacktoberfest is all about building brand-new projects with open-source AI and open-weight models. Here's everything you need to know about Hacktoberfest 2026. Missed Week 3: Slow and Steady ? No problem. Every challenge is a fresh start, so you're competing on the same footing as everyone else. This week, we'll select one overall winner and a winner in each of our 20 partner categories . See all the challenges and current partner categories on the HF26 DEV Challenge Hub . Build something spooky, or something that honors the past in the spirit of Día de los Muertos, with open-weight models or open-source AI. This week brings us Halloween on October 31 and Día de los Muertos on November 1 and 2 , a stretch of the calendar when the line between past and present feels a little thinner. Whether that brings to mind things that go bump in the night, ofrendas glowing with candlelight and marigolds, or the memories and stories we carry with us, we want to see what it inspires you to build. The theme is intentionally broad, so interpret it however you'd like! That can mean running an open-weight model, building on an open-source agent harness or framework, running inference locally, or all three. Whatever you pick, the open pieces should be what makes your project work. In your post, tell us why open innovation matters for what you built . Does running your own model mean your project works with the lights (and the internet) off? Keep your family's photos and stories private and on your own machine? Make sure what you build isn't locked inside a service that might disappear someday? Tell us where your open-based approach worked better than a closed one. Ghost in the Machine Submission Template Alongside our overall winner, we have 20 prize categories for projects that use a specific partner's technology. You don't need to use any of these to win the overall prize, but if you've been curious about any of this tech, this is a great excuse to give one a try. Full descriptions are on the hub . Pro Tip: Partner category winners come from a smaller pool of submissions, so your odds are meaningfully higher. Note: One project can enter every category it genuinely uses, but you can only win once per challenge, and we'll aim to celebrate as many different builders as possible across the month. Free credits: several partners are giving participants credits and promo codes. Claim yours at hacktoberfest.com/my . A huge thank you to our partners for making these prizes possible! This is DEV, so your write-up matters most . Show your work. We'd love to see how you built it. Save your agent session with DevRelay and embed it in your post, or link to it. It's optional, but it helps the judges understand your process. All participants with a valid submission will receive a completion badge. Publish a post on DEV using the submission template above. Tell us what you built and how you interpreted the theme, show us a demo, and explain why open innovation matters for what you built. If you can show us the moment your project landed, whether it gave someone chills or brought back a memory, even better! Please review our judging criteria, rules, guidelines, and FAQ page before submitting so you understand our participation guidelines and official contest rules, such as eligibility requirements. This is the last challenge of our Hacktoberfest series , and we've loved seeing everything you've built with open-source AI this month. Thank you to every participant, partner, and community member who showed up week after week. Let's make this final week one to remember! Questions about the challenge? Drop them in the comments below. Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use. A haunted terminal that digs through git history and tells you why a suspicious line exists would be fun. Especially when the ghost turns out to be your own commit from three years ago. Bonus points if it cites the commit before accusing you 😂 The strongest projects will probably be the ones that balance a creative idea with a clear technical reason for using open models. A spooky demo might catch attention, but showing how the model works, where it struggles, and what the developer learned could make the submission much more convincing.
